newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: FOCUS - Iraq, US steps bring oil deal closer, maybe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Iraq, US steps bring oil deal closer, maybe.

text.p: Prospects for ending the torturous guessing game of when the Iraq-U.N. oil-for-food deal will become reality seemed to improve greatly Monday after Iraq dropped demands on the plan's structure.
Three key players released positive statements, moving the onus of getting the plan operational from the political to the technical arena, at least for the time being.

Iraq told the United Nations it unconditionally accepted the oil plan; the United States said it would now approve a pricing formula for regulating oil sales; and U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said he was "optimistic" for movement on the deal in a few weeks.

One of the issues that has been delaying the deal were Iraqi demands that it control the number, make-up and freedom of movement of a U.N. team meant to monitor the accord. These concerns were "formally" removed by Iraq's move today.
U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Madeleine Albright stated the U.S. would "act positively" on the pricing formula now that Iraq was on board for the logistics of the plan.

These facts would seemingly be enough to dramatically depress oil prices, but prices did not slide sharply, reflecting the extreme skepticism associated with any news on what has become the ultimate game of crying wolf.
The deal was close to implementation in late August when Baghdad sent troops into the north of Iraq to aid Kurdish "allies," forcing the plan's suspension.
In addition to general wariness about Saddam, the timing of Iraq's acquiescence at the beginning of OPEC meeting in Vienna tweaked the oil market's curiosity.
"Iraq tends to come out with statements about the deal around OPEC meetings to pressure prices," said Tom Bentz, oil analyst for ING Derivatives.

NYMEX spot January crude futures made lows at $23.25 a barrel after Iraq said it accepted the oil plan. But, prices recovered to unchanged levels, supporting sentiment that until the deal was delivered there would be no rapid sell-off.
Western diplomats blamed Saddam Hussein's penchant for unpreditability as cause for concern, and noted there was still plenty of room for snafus to delay oil sales.
Still, the momentum was seen leaning to getting a final deal in the near-term.

"There are are a number of operational and technical steps to be taken, but there's nothing that we know of that can't be done in short order," said a U.S. State Department official, who added that short order meant "right away."
Iraq's Hamdoon said all that remained before oil sales could start was approval of the December pricing formula.
The U.N. Security Council sanctions panel should receive the pricing plan by the end of this week, after U.N.-appointed oil experts, or overseers, have time to comment.

The vote on the formula will be done by a "no-objection" procedure, thus no formal meeting of the sanctions panel is necessary. Still, the German delegates who chair the committee were said to be in favor of a formal meeting, possibly as early as Monday, December 2, diplomats said.
Once the formula is approved -- as most now predict it will be -- the secretariat must report to the Security Council that all steps have been finalized.

To further the technical tasks remaining, the Dutch firm Saybolt will launch an inspection of oil metering equipment on December 5, specifically to ensure faulty equipment at the Zakho station along the Iraq-Turkey border is operational.
Lloyds of London personnel were also to inspect facilities this week, to ensure its ability to moitor aid imports.
Both companies were expected to report back to the United Nations by mid-December, possibly allowing Boutros-Ghali to report by year's end.
Boutros-Ghali's term expires December 31, lending much import to getting the oil-for-food deal finalized ahead of what might be his final days in office, a diplomat said.
